prompt:
A laminated loading card of the sort a quarry weighbridge office makes up for one regular lorry and hands to the shovel driver. One card, drawn in plain line work: a section straight through the tipper body seen from the side, with the printed panel of figures beneath it.

The body on this lorry is a taper: 1200 mm long by 1000 mm wide on the floor, opening out to 5600 mm by 2800 mm at the rim, and 1500 mm deep. Ten level marks are painted up the inside of its front bulkhead, numbered 1 at the bottom to 10 at the rim, one every 150 mm.

The panel beneath the section already carries the two figures the office holds for this job: the lorry's plated payload of 10.0 tonnes, and the bulk density of the material at 1.50 tonnes per cubic metre. It has one more line on it, headed LOAD TO MARK, waiting for a number.

Draw the section with the load hatched in to the level this lorry may be loaded to on this material, and fill in the LOAD TO MARK line. Which mark that is, is for you to work out -- I am deliberately not telling you, and I am not telling you what the body holds.

The card goes into the cab as drawn, so nothing may be added that does the reading for the driver: no arrow, no ring drawn round a mark, no dimension line up the bulkhead, no note in the margin and no writing anywhere on the card other than the mark numbers, the panel of figures and the LOAD TO MARK line.
easy_question: Never mind how well it is drawn. Does this picture show a drawing of a container seen in section with numbered marks up one side of it? A drawing, a scan or a photograph ALL count as yes. Answer NO only if the image shows a blank sheet that just states an answer, or shows no container at all. Answer yes or no only.
